newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan seen echoing upbeat economic assessment.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan seen echoing upbeat economic assessment.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan testifies to Congress on Thursday for the second time in two weeks, and Fed sources said they expect him to echo last week's generally upbeat remarks on the economy.
Still, financial markets will listen closely for fresh signals about whether the Fed is close to raisling official U.S. interest rates.
Much of Greenspan's opening statement to the Senate Finance Committee is likely to focus on the consumer price index -- the Fed chief believes it overstates inflation.
His opening statement is also expected to address proposals to privatize Social Security.

His economic assessment is expected to echo the one he gave the Senate Budget Committee last week: generally upbeat but with a warning about the risk of faster inflation in the future from stepped-up wage demands.

Since then, the government has reported that wages and benefits rose 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter, after a 0.6 percent increase in the third. For 1996 as a whole, worker compensation grew 2.9 percent, up from 2.7 percent in 1995.
Stock and bond prices bounded ahead initially on Wednesday on news of the smaller-than-expected rise in fourth quarter compensation, then fell back before rebounding in a choppy day of trading.

A Fed source warned the markets' early enthusiasm about the data may have been overdone. Wage growth picked up last year, rising at their fastest clip since 1991, and the gains were widespread, the source, who declined to be named, noted.
The overall compensation rise was more muted as health benefits rose more slowly. But the Fed source questioned how long that can last if labor markets remain tight.
"Overall, things look fairly favorable in terms of the expansion, hopefully not too favorable so that we don't get any more pressure on the labor market," another source said.

The economy looks to have ended 1996 on a strong note, but it remains unclear how much of that strength will be carried over into this year. Much of the fourth quarter's buoyancy was due to stronger-than-expected net exports, but part of that may represent a problem with the seasonal adjustment factors.
Several sources said they do not see any big risk of the economy taking off and triggering a burst of inflation.
"It's kind of hard to argue we're going to be off to the races," one Fed source said.

But that does not mean the Fed can relax, sources said. Even modest growth this year of 2-1/2 percent would pose a dilemma for the Fed because it would likely mean a further tightening of labor markets and a greater risk of inflation.
Richmond Fed President Al Broaddus said earlier this week that the risks to the economy were tilted "somewhat to the upside" primarily because of the stretched labor market.

Fed sources said the strength of the dollar -- it rose to a 47-month high against the Japanese yen earlier today in Tokyo -- though should help contain inflation by holding down import prices and restraining exports.
Greenspan last week said that imports provided a "safety valve" for the U.S. economy last year.
A majority of economists polled by Reuters expect the Fed to tighten credit near the middle of this year.
